questions.topic: Holding a position at its strongest

options.text: Stating the case in the form that a fair-minded listener would find hardest to dismiss.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Reconstructing the strongest rejected view
questions.learningObjective: Reconstruct the strongest version of a rejected option
questions.stem: Explain how an architect should reconstruct a site option that the studio has decided against.

answer.exemplar: The architect should begin from the option's strongest version rather than its first draft: what would this plan do best, for whom, and under what conditions, and can each of those be met on this site. The reconstruction is fair only if it can be defended by someone who prefers that option, and every step should be recorded so a reader can check that nothing was smuggled in. Then the comparison is made on the same criteria for both options, since a comparison built for one side to win settles nothing.

questions.explanation: The strongest rejected view is reconstructed by stating what it would do best and whether the site allows it. Rebuilding the weakest version makes the comparison worthless.
questions.hint: Ask what the rejected option would do best.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Terms that shift sense mid-argument
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a term that changes sense mid-argument
questions.stem: Explain how a term can shift sense in the middle of an architect's brief without the author noticing.

answer.exemplar: A term shifts sense when the same word is used in two slightly different senses and the argument quietly borrows the force of the second while resting on the first. In a brief this often happens with words like open, light or flexible, which start as descriptions of a physical condition and end as claims about how people will feel. Nothing on the page marks the change, so the reader experiences a continuous argument, but the second half of the argument is actually about something different from the first, and the conclusion inherits a certainty it has not earned.

questions.explanation: The sense shifts when one word serves two meanings and the argument borrows the second's force while resting on the first. It reads as continuous, but the conclusion inherits unearned certainty.
questions.hint: Look for one word doing two different jobs.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Narrowing a topic in two steps
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a two-step narrowing from a one-step narrowing
questions.stem: Explain what makes a two-step narrowing different from a one-step narrowing in a design brief.

answer.exemplar: A one-step narrowing replaces the broad request with a single narrower request, which is useful but still leaves the team with a whole subject to address. A two-step narrowing first breaks the request into parts, then chooses one part to work on, and the second step is what makes the work bounded. The parts must genuinely divide the subject rather than merely restate it, and the chosen part must be one on which the studio has some authority to act, otherwise the narrowing has produced a question nobody can answer.

questions.explanation: The second step in a two-step narrowing bounds the work, since the first only divides the subject and the second commits to a part. If the parts merely restate the whole, nothing has been narrowed.
questions.hint: Check that the second step actually commits.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Sympathetic reading of a weak argument
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish sympathetic reading from agreement
questions.stem: Explain why reading a weak argument sympathetically is not the same as agreeing with it.

answer.exemplar: A sympathetic reading is a reconstruction of what the argument would look like if it were well made, and it asks the reader to judge the reasoning rather than the polish. Agreeing with it is a separate verdict on the conclusion. The two come apart in useful ways: an argument can be sympathetic and still rest on a premise the studio rejects, in which case the disagreement is precise and worth having, and an argument can be brilliantly argued and still wrong. A brief that reads weak proposals sympathetically therefore reaches better conclusions, not milder ones.

questions.explanation: A sympathetic reading reconstructs what the argument would look like if it were well made, and asks the reader to judge the reasoning, not the polish. Agreement is a separate verdict on the claim.
questions.hint: Reconstructing the reasoning is not endorsing the claim.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Holding a position at its strongest
questions.learningObjective: Explain what holding a position at its strongest means
questions.stem: Explain what it means to hold a design position at its strongest.

answer.exemplar: Holding a position at its strongest means giving the case in the form that would survive the most competent objection, so that the reader cannot dismiss it for how it was put rather than for what it claims. In practice that means stating the aim plainly, choosing the reasons that bear most directly on that aim, and acknowledging the limitations that a fair reader would notice before raising them. It does not mean omitting difficulties, because a case that hides its weakness has not been strengthened, it has only been hidden from the person testing it.

questions.explanation: Holding the position at its strongest means stating the aim and the reasons that bear on it in the form that survives objection. Hiding difficulties weakens rather than strengthens the case.
questions.hint: Ask how the case would fare before an opponent.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Sequence of the framing steps
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the order of framing steps matters
questions.stem: Explain why the order of the framing steps in a brief matters to the reader.

answer.exemplar: The order tells the reader what kind of thing each passage is, and it changes what can be understood from it. A scope statement placed after the reasons leaves the reader unsure whether the reasons are being offered as proof or illustration, and a qualification separated from the claim it limits leaves the reader to decide which claim it applies to, which they cannot do reliably. Working back from the conclusion compounds the problem, because the reasons are then selected for their support of the conclusion rather than for their bearing on the aim, and the brief stops being an argument and becomes a case.

questions.explanation: Order tells the reader what kind of passage each part is. Misplaced scope or qualifications leave them unable to judge what supports what, and working backwards selects reasons for agreement.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader can tell from each passage's place.

answer.exemplar: The reader needs enough to locate the exact evidence and see it in its original setting. questions.topic: Terms that shift sense mid-argument

questions.stem: Explain how a shifting term can give a brief an argument that looks stronger than it is.

answer.exemplar: When a term changes sense in the middle of an argument, the earlier half is usually doing careful descriptive work and the later half is claiming something larger, and the shared word lets the reader carry the modesty of the first half into the confidence of the second. The result is an inference the author never actually made but which the reader completes, and it is hard to challenge because each half of the brief looks reasonable on its own. This is why the drift is worth hunting: the conclusion is often credited with a certainty that belongs to the descriptive half only.

questions.explanation: A drifting term lets a descriptive half carry its restraint into a bolder later claim, so the reader completes an inference the author never made. Each half looks reasonable alone, hiding the slide.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Narrowing a topic in two steps
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a two-step narrowing beats a one-step narrowing
questions.stem: Explain why narrowing a design topic in two steps is usually better than narrowing it in one.

answer.exemplar: A single narrowing step replaces the broad request with a narrower request, which sounds like progress but leaves the studio with a subject rather than a question, since a narrowed subject can still contain several investigations and several answers. The two-step version divides the subject first, so the second step is a choice among identifiable parts, and that choice can be checked: a reader can see which part was taken and ask whether that was the right one. It also makes the discarded parts visible, which is often where the client's real concern was hiding, and that discovery would have been lost if the first step had jumped straight to a narrower subject.

questions.explanation: One step narrows the subject but may still contain several investigations, while two steps force a checkable choice among parts. The second step reveals the discarded parts, where a concern may hide.
questions.hint: Ask whether the result is a question or still a subject.

questions.explanation: The scope and aim determine which reasons matter and in what order the reader needs them, so they come first and everything else follows. Deciding the conclusion first reverses the frame.
questions.hint: Settle scope and aim, then sequence the rest.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Terms that shift sense mid-argument
questions.learningObjective: Identify the consequence of a term shifting sense
questions.stem: What is the consequence of a term shifting sense in the middle of an argument?

options.text: The conclusion inherits certainty from the part of the argument that was better supported.
The argument becomes shorter, because the second sense carries the whole point.
options.misconception: suggests the drift makes a brief more concise

options.text: The brief must be rewritten entirely before any part of it can be cited.
options.misconception: claims the defect ruins every use of the text

options.text: The earlier part of the argument is invalidated, since it used the wrong sense.
options.misconception: assumes the first use was the mistaken one

questions.explanation: A drifting term lets the firmer earlier part lend its confidence to the later claim, so the conclusion appears better supported than it is. The defect is not brevity or total invalidation.
questions.hint: Ask which half lends its certainty to the other.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Holding a position at its strongest
questions.learningObjective: Explain why hiding weaknesses weakens a case
questions.stem: Explain why a case that hides its weaknesses is weaker than one that states them.

answer.exemplar: A hidden weakness is not removed by being unmentioned, it is merely unavailable for the reader to weigh, and a reader who suspects it will discount the whole case rather than the particular point. Stating a limitation in the right place does the opposite: it shows the author knows which part of the argument is strongest and which part is not, and it lets the reader accept the reasons that carry the weight while discounting only what fails. This is why a brief that names its weak joint is generally trusted further than one that presents an unbroken case with no acknowledged difficulty.

questions.explanation: A hidden weakness is merely unavailable for the reader to weigh, and a suspicion of it discounts the whole case. Naming the weak joint shows which parts carry the weight, so those can be judged.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader does with an unmentioned weakness.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Reconstructing the strongest rejected view
questions.learningObjective: Reconstruct the strongest version of a rejected option

stimulus.body: The studio rejected the sawtooth roof for the workshop and wrote that it would cost more and complicate the gutters. The site is flat and open to the north, the budget was fixed in outline, and the client wants daylight deep into the plan.

questions.stem: Which question set rebuilds the strongest case for the option the studio rejected?

options.text: Would the sawtooth roof have given more useful roof area for plant?
options.misconception: asks about a secondary benefit, not the main grounds

options.text: What could a sawtooth roof do for the client deep daylight that a flat roof cannot?
Which gutter details would the sawtooth roof have required?
options.misconception: focuses on the practical objection the studio recorded

options.text: How much would the sawtooth roof have added to the budget?
options.misconception: fixes the reconstruction on cost, which the studio rejected

questions.explanation: The strongest grounds for the sawtooth roof lie in the deep daylight the client asked for, which the second option reconstructs. Roof area, gutter details and price repeat existing reasons.
questions.hint: Ask what it could do for the client's stated wish.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Sympathetic reading of a weak argument
questions.learningObjective: Repair a weak justification in a brief
questions.stem: How would you revise the weak justification in the brief so it supports its proposal properly?

options.text: Add a second justification, so the proposal has more support than before.
options.misconception: piles up reasons without repairing the weak one

options.text: Remove the justification, so the proposal is carried by the drawings alone.
options.misconception: deletes the reasoning instead of reconstructing it

options.text: Replace it with a study of similar buildings, which carries more weight.
options.misconception: substitutes precedent for the proposal's own reasoning

options.text: State the aim the proposal serves, then give the reasoning that connects the aim to the move.

questions.explanation: The repair states the aim and supplies the reasoning that connects it to the design move, giving the proposal a case it can be judged on. Adding a reason or importing precedent leaves the flaw.
questions.hint: Name the aim, then supply the reasoning.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Citations that let a reader find the claim
questions.learningObjective: Make a citation findable for a reader
questions.stem: Which pair of moves would make the brief's citations findable for a reader?

options.text: Identify the source in full, then mark the page or figure where the claim appears.
Name the author and the year, then rely on the reader's own library skills.
options.misconception: gives partial details and leaves the search to the reader

options.text: Collect the sources into a numbered list, then number the claims in the text.
options.misconception: numbers sources without saying where in them the claim sits

options.text: Ask the team which sources they trust most, and cite only those.
options.misconception: filters by standing rather than by the location of evidence

questions.explanation: A citation is findable when it names the source completely and marks the place inside it where the claim sits. Partial details, a numbered list and a trust filter lead nowhere.
questions.hint: Name the source, then mark the place.
